title: The new moon
tomorrow: a new year with no countdown and no fireworks. how does it start?

cards: Your phone can tell you the moon's phase to the minute. People in Medina had to look up, and they asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about it: these new moons, what are they? The Qur'an answers, and then does something strange.
In the very same verse, it starts talking about doors, and about people who came into their own houses from the back. A question about the sky. An answer about doors.

teach.b: First the answer itself, in Pickthall's words: "They ask thee, (O Muhammad), of new moons, say: They are fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage."
Not what the moon is made of, but what it's for: a clock that belongs to everyone, no device required. Now the doors.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, al-Bara' explains that some people of Medina, coming home from pilgrimage, wouldn't walk in through their front doors; they climbed in from the back, as a pious custom.
The verse answers them too: righteousness isn't coming in the back way; it's being mindful of God. So come in through the doors. Put the two halves together and the puzzle clears.
A question about the sky gets an answer about life on the ground. The moon marks the months; what counts is how you walk through them. And the month begins with looking.
In another report in Bukhari, he says: fast when you see it, and break the fast when you see it; if cloud hides it, complete the count.
When the crescent appears, a report in Jami' at-Tirmidhi gives a short du'a for it, and it ends by speaking to the moon itself: my Lord and your Lord is God.
Here's the one to tell a friend: the du'a greets the moon as a fellow creature. Communities still differ on sighting by eye or by calculation, but looking up is where it started.

how: Muslims watch for the new crescent after sunset near the end of each lunar month, especially before Ramadan and the Eids; some communities follow a local sighting, others an announced sighting or an astronomical calculation.

games.q: your little brother asks why Ramadan moves to a different time every year. what's the simplest true answer?
o: the months follow the moon, so they move against the sun's calendar.

games.why: the Qur'an calls the new moons fixed seasons for people: Islamic months follow the moon, so they travel through the solar year.

practice: If you can see the sky, look for the moon now. If not, go to a window and find the patch of western sky where a new crescent would sit just after sunset. Look at that one place, steadily, for as long as the sit runs.

wordCard.voice: The new moon, the hilal: the thin crescent after sunset that begins each Islamic month, watched for by eye.

orig.note: Arabic: hilal, the crescent of a new moon; its plural, ahilla, is the word in 2:189.

carryVoice: Pocket this: a new month begins when someone looks up and sees it. Day two of fourteen.
